response:
I have not settled the full uniqueness claim. I do have a grid-specific structural result that substantially narrows it:If a flexible endpoint has at least two neighbors in  $T$ , then some replacement matching admits a feasible bundle of exactly two promoted endpoints.Consequently, in an exchange-terminal pair, every endpoint with at least two  $T$ -neighbors has a globally forced matching partner. Moreover, every nonempty connected component of  $G[P]$  has a vertex of  $P$ -degree one in each checkerboard color.The remaining case is precise: forced matching edges can potentially transmit the freezing process into a nontrivial allowed-edge component through a degree-four vertex. The argument below handles direct obstruction by selections, but does not establish that such transmission through forced edges is impossible.1. Definitions and elementary matching factsWrite
$$H=G[P],\qquad A=T\cup P,\qquad
d_A(v)=|\Gamma_G(v)\cap A|.$$
An edge of  $H$  is allowed if it belongs to some perfect matching of  $H$ . An endpoint is flexible if its matching partner differs between two perfect matchings. Otherwise its matching edge is forced, meaning that edge belongs to every perfect matching.A vertex of occupied degree at most two can be promoted by itself under any perfect matching: deleting its mate leaves at most one occupied neighbor. Thus exchange-terminality implies
$$d_A(p)\ge 3\qquad(p\in P).
\tag{1}$$
We will use the connected components of the graph consisting of all allowed edges. Here are the relevant facts, with their justification.Fix a perfect matching
$$N=\{b_iw_i:i\in I\},$$
where  $b_i$  is black and  $w_i$  is white. Contract each matching edge to its index  $i$ , and replace every nonmatching edge  $b_iw_j$  by a directed edge
$$i\longrightarrow j.$$
A nonmatching edge is allowed exactly when its directed edge lies on a directed cycle. Indeed, a directed cycle expands to an  $N$ -alternating cycle, which can be flipped. Conversely, the symmetric difference of  $N$  with a perfect matching containing the edge supplies such an alternating cycle.It follows that:The allowed-edge components are exactly the strongly connected components of this directed graph, with their matched pairs restored.Every  $H$ -edge whose endpoints lie in the same allowed-edge component is allowed.Every perfect matching restricts to a perfect matching on each allowed-edge component. These restrictions can be chosen independently and recombined.A component consisting of one matched pair is a forced edge. In every larger allowed-edge component, every endpoint is flexible and has at least two allowed neighbors.Directing edges between distinct components from their black endpoint’s component to their white endpoint’s component gives an acyclic condensation graph.The independence in item 3 is only between distinct allowed-edge components. We will not assume that two allowed edges within one component can necessarily occur together.2. Main grid lemma: a flexible endpoint with two selection neighbors unlocks a squareLemmaSuppose  $(T,P)$  is feasible and satisfies (1). If a flexible endpoint  $p$  has at least two neighbors in  $T$ , then some perfect matching of  $H$  admits a feasible promotion bundle with  $|X|=2$ .ProofBecause  $p$  is flexible, it has at least two allowed neighbors in  $P$ . The grid has maximum degree four. Therefore  $p$  has exactly two neighbors in  $P$  and exactly two neighbors in  $T$ .First, its two  $P$ -neighbors cannot be opposite.For example, suppose its  $P$ -neighbors are east and west, and its  $T$ -neighbors are north and south. Both transverse neighbors of the eastern  $P$ -neighbor are then adjacent to one of those selections. Since each selection already has  $p$  as an occupied neighbor, feasibility forces both transverse positions to be unoccupied.The eastern endpoint would have at most two occupied neighbors:  $p$  and its eastern neighbor. This contradicts (1).After a grid symmetry and translation, we may therefore write
$$p=(0,0),\qquad q=(1,0),\qquad r=(0,1),$$
with
$$(-1,0),(0,-1)\in T.
\tag{2}$$
Selection feasibility gives
$$(1,-1),(-1,1)\notin A.
\tag{3}$$
The endpoint  $q$  has one unoccupied grid neighbor by (3). Condition (1) therefore forces all its other grid neighbors to be occupied. The same holds for  $r$ . Hence, writing
$$s=(1,1),\qquad v=(2,0),\qquad w=(0,2),$$
we have
$$s,v,w\in A,\qquad d_A(q)=d_A(r)=3.
\tag{4}$$
Moreover,
$$s\in P,
\tag{5}$$
because  $s$  is adjacent to both occupied vertices  $q,r$ , so it cannot belong to  $T$ .We have obtained a full endpoint square
$$p,q,s,r.$$
It remains to show that this square is alternating under some perfect matching.Let  $C$  be the allowed-edge component containing  $p$ . Since  $p$  is flexible and has only  $q,r$  as  $P$ -neighbors, both  $pq$  and  $pr$  are allowed. Thus
$$p,q,r\in C.$$
I claim that  $s\in C$ .Suppose instead that  $s\notin C$ . Then  $qs$  and  $rs$  are disallowed. Since  $q$  is flexible and its only other occupied neighbors are  $p,v$ , it follows that
$$v\in P,\qquad qv\text{ is allowed}.
\tag{6}$$
Similarly,
$$w\in P,\qquad rw\text{ is allowed}.
\tag{7}$$
In any perfect matching,  $s$  cannot be matched to  $q$  or  $r$ . Its mate must therefore be one of
$$u=(2,1),\qquad z=(1,2).$$
Suppose first that some perfect matching contains  $su$ . Choose a perfect matching containing  $qv$ . Recombine its restriction to  $C$  with the first matching’s restrictions to all other allowed-edge components. This produces a perfect matching containing both
$$qv,\qquad su.$$
These are opposite edges of the unit square with vertices
$$q=(1,0),\ v=(2,0),\ u=(2,1),\ s=(1,1).$$
Because  $G$  is the induced nearest-neighbor grid, the other two square edges also exist. Flipping the square gives a perfect matching containing  $qs$ , contradicting that  $qs$  is disallowed.If  $s$  is instead matched to  $z$ , the same argument uses  $rw$  and the square
$$r,w,z,s.$$
It produces a perfect matching containing  $rs$ , again a contradiction.Thus  $s\in C$ .Now  $qs$  is an  $H$ -edge internal to an allowed-edge component, so it is allowed. Choose a perfect matching  $N_*$  containing  $qs$ . Since  $p$  has only  $q,r$  as  $P$ -neighbors,  $N_*$  must also contain  $pr$ .Set
$$X=\{q,r\},\qquad Y=\{s,p\}.$$
These are two distinct matching edges, with one endpoint promoted from each. By (4), each promoted endpoint has occupied degree three, and each loses both  $p$  and  $s$ . Therefore
$$d_{A\setminus Y}(q)=d_{A\setminus Y}(r)=1.$$
The bundle is feasible. ∎This proof uses both special features that an arbitrary bipartite-graph argument would miss: the vacancies forced by the degree-one condition on selections, and the square edges supplied by the induced grid.3. Consequences for every exchange-terminal pair3.1 Every endpoint with two selection neighbors has a forced partnerThe lemma immediately gives
$$|\Gamma_G(p)\cap T|\ge2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p\text{ has a forced matching partner}
\tag{8}$$
in an exchange-terminal pair.Equivalently, every flexible endpoint satisfies
$$|\Gamma_G(p)\cap T|\le1.
\tag{9}$$
This excludes a natural potential counterexample mechanism: an alternating component cannot be frozen directly by placing two selections next to one of its endpoints.There must nevertheless be endpoints with at least two selection neighbors in both colors whenever  $P\ne\varnothing$ . For if every black endpoint had at most one  $T$ -neighbor, promoting all black endpoints and deleting all their white mates would be feasible under every perfect matching. The white case is symmetric. By (8), these initial obstructions must all be forced endpoints.3.2 Every connected endpoint component has a leaf of each colorHere “leaf” means degree one in  $H=G[P]$ , not occupied degree one.CorollaryIn an exchange-terminal feasible grid pair, every nonempty connected component of  $H$  contains a black  $H$ -leaf and a white  $H$ -leaf.More precisely, every source and every sink in the allowed-edge condensation consists of a single forced matching edge.ProofConsider a source allowed-edge component  $C$ . By the orientation of the condensation, there is no  $H$ -edge from a black endpoint outside  $C$  to a white endpoint inside  $C$ . Consequently every  $P$ -neighbor of a white endpoint of  $C$  lies in  $C$ .Suppose  $C$  is nontrivial. Every endpoint in  $C$  is flexible, so (9) gives
$$|\Gamma_G(w)\cap T|\le1
\qquad(w\in C\cap W).$$
Under any perfect matching, promote
$$X=C\cap W$$
and delete
$$Y=C\cap B.$$
Every  $P$ -neighbor of every promoted endpoint is deleted. At most its one  $T$ -neighbor remains. This is a nonempty feasible bundle, a contradiction.Thus every source component is a single forced matching edge. Its white endpoint has no  $P$ -neighbor outside that edge, and hence has  $H$ -degree one.The color-reversed argument shows that every sink is a single forced matching edge whose black endpoint has  $H$ -degree one.Apply this separately to each connected component of  $H$ : its finite condensation has a source and a sink. ∎This settles some substantial special cases. In particular:An exchange-terminal  $H$  cannot have a nonempty connected component of minimum degree at least two.An isolated nontrivial allowed-edge component always permits a bundle.A counterexample to uniqueness must have nontrivial allowed-edge components lying between forced components in the condensation.The leaf condition alone does not eliminate those interior nontrivial components.3.3 The forced leaves have constrained grid geometryUnder (1), an endpoint cannot have two opposite  $T$ -neighbors. Any matching mate in either remaining direction would then have both transverse positions forced unoccupied, giving it occupied degree at most two.It follows that every  $H$ -leaf has exactly two perpendicular  $T$ -neighbors and occupied degree exactly three. Relative to its mate, one selection lies directly behind the leaf and the other lies in a transverse direction. Its mate also has occupied degree exactly three: the transverse selection forces one of the mate’s neighboring positions to be unoccupied.Thus the source and sink edges in the corollary come with specific boundary geometry; they are not arbitrary pendant edges.4. Exact location of the unresolved propagation stepThe following fixed-point formulation makes the remaining issue precise.First, every feasible bundle contains a feasible monochromatic bundle. If a bundle promotes both colors, retaining only its black promoted endpoints and their white mates preserves the feasibility inequalities at those black endpoints. The deleted black mates associated with white promotions were never neighbors of the black promoted endpoints. The white case is symmetric.Fix a perfect matching  $N$ , and consider black promotions. Start with
$$E_0=\varnothing,$$
and repeatedly eliminate a black endpoint  $b$  whenever
$$\left|\Gamma_G(b)\cap\bigl(T\cup N(E_k)\bigr)\right|\ge2.$$
Thus
$$E_{k+1}
=
E_k\cup
\left\{
b\in P\cap B:
\left|\Gamma_G(b)\cap\bigl(T\cup N(E_k)\bigr)\right|\ge2
\right\}.
\tag{10}$$
Let  $E_\infty$  be the eventual fixed point. Then
$$S=(P\cap B)\setminus E_\infty
\tag{11}$$
is the greatest feasible black promotion set.Indeed, at termination each  $b\in S$  has at most one neighbor in
$$T\cup N(E_\infty),$$
which is exactly the set of its occupied neighbors that remain after deleting  $N(S)$ . Conversely, no feasible black promotion set can contain an eliminated vertex: induction through (10) shows that such a vertex would have at least two neighbors remaining outside the deleted mate set.Consequently,
$$\text{no black bundle under }N
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
E_\infty=P\cap B.
\tag{12}$$
Together with the white process, this is an exact freezing criterion.Now suppose, provisionally, that an exchange-terminal counterexample exists. Run (10) sequentially under any perfect matching and consider the first eliminated flexible black endpoint  $b$ .Every previously eliminated black endpoint is forced. Therefore its mate is also globally fixed. Furthermore,  $b$  has at least two allowed neighbors in its own nontrivial allowed-edge component, and neither of those neighbors can yet be the mate of an eliminated endpoint.For  $b$  to be eliminated, it must have at least two additional occupied neighbors already in the persistent set. The degree-four bound forces the following exact configuration:
$$\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
d_A(b)&=4,\\
b&\text{ has exactly two neighbors in its own allowed component},\\
b&\text{ has exactly two occupied neighbors outside that component},\\
\text{both outside neighbors}&\text{ are already persistent.}
\end{aligned}}
\tag{13}$$
Those outside neighbors belong to  $T$  or are mates of previously eliminated forced endpoints. By the main lemma, they cannot both belong to  $T$ . At least one must be an endpoint of a forced matching edge.Thus the remaining obstruction has only these two forms at its first entry:One original selection and one persistent endpoint of a forced matching edge.Two persistent endpoints of forced matching edges.A degree-three flexible endpoint cannot be the first entry.There is also a useful local restriction on the forced edges involved. If  $u$  is a forced neighbor of a flexible vertex  $b$ , and  $a$  is an allowed neighbor of  $b$  perpendicular to  $u$ , then the forced mate of  $u$  cannot be the fourth corner
$$u+(a-b)$$
of that unit square. Otherwise a matching containing  $ba$ , together with the forced edge at  $u$ , makes the square alternating; flipping it contradicts forcedness. In particular, when the two allowed neighbors of  $b$  are opposite, a forced blocker in either remaining direction must be matched straight outward.5. What remains open in this answerThe step still needed for a positive answer is:Show that freezing propagation from the original feasible selections, through globally forced matching edges, cannot freeze every replacement matching of a nontrivial allowed-edge component.The square lemma proves this when the two blocking neighbors are original selections. It does not prove it when one or both are persistent endpoints of forced matching edges. Those endpoints may have several occupied neighbors, so treating them as new selections would violate the hypothesis that drives the local geometry.Accordingly, the proven progress is the flexible-endpoint lemma, the forced source/sink result, and the leaf conclusion for every connected endpoint component. The full exchange-terminal uniqueness claim remains unresolved here, specifically in the degree-four propagation case (13).
assessment: Partial structural research, not an independent review of the later counterexample. Its full uniqueness question was left unresolved in this answer and has separately been refuted by our core and all-parameter positive graft.
